title: Integrating Calcium Imaging, Pupillometry, and Locomotion Tracking in Mice
author: Ortiz-Juza, Tormes-Vaquerano, et al.

steps.title: Assemble head‑fixation hardware
steps.instruction: Mount the optical breadboard and install the rotary (quadrature) encoder, locomotion wheel, headplates, pupil CMOS camera, waste‑management ramp, and microscope objective, keeping their relative positions fixed for the entire experiment.

steps.title: Build Arduino shield
steps.instruction: Solder the custom printed circuit board (Arduino shield) with a real‑time clock module and external trigger connectors, then connect it to the Arduino microcontroller to provide digital interfacing and timestamping for all devices.

steps.title: Prepare aluminum head‑rings
steps.instruction: Fabricate and clean aluminum head‑rings that will later be attached to the mouse skull for head‑fixation.

steps.title: Implant GRIN relay lens
steps.instruction: Perform the surgical protocol to implant the gradient‑refractive‑index (GRIN) relay lens into the target subcortical region and secure the prepared head‑ring onto the skull.

steps.title: Habituate mice to system
steps.instruction: Acclimate mice to the head‑fixation apparatus over multiple sessions until they remain calm during head‑fixation.

steps.title: Position imaging objective
steps.instruction: Raise the multiphoton objective approximately 28 cm from the air table to create space for the head‑ring, then adjust the objective‑to‑head‑ring distance to reach the desired imaging depth beneath the implanted GRIN lens.

steps.title: Detach components after imaging
steps.instruction: After each imaging session, remove the waste‑management ramp and the locomotion wheel from the main base to allow cleaning or system adjustments.

steps.title: Extract pupil dynamics with DLC
steps.instruction: Record pupil video with the CMOS camera, run DeepLabCut to obtain x‑y coordinates for eight eye landmarks, then apply the R function TransformDLC using (i) two spatial calibration points and (ii) the DLC .csv file; compute the pixel‑to‑mm conversion ratio by dividing the measured pixel distance between calibration points by the 3.6 mm reference distance, multiply all coordinates by this ratio, calculate pupil diameter as the average distance between opposite points, filter by DLC confidence score, interpolate during blinks, and finally normalize each mouse’s pupil size to the maximum diameter observed during the first few seconds of the experiment.

steps.title: Convert wheel encoder data
steps.instruction: Import the rotary encoder output, run the R function TransformWheel with the wheel diameter (as specified for your hardware) to compute wheel circumference, divide by the encoder resolution to obtain distance traveled per tick, and calculate velocity; optionally compute additional locomotion metrics using the provided custom code.

steps.title: Process calcium imaging data
steps.instruction: Run the CaImAn pipeline on the recorded multiphoton movies, scale each neuron’s fluorescence by its trial‑wise standard deviation, bin the resulting activity in 1‑second intervals, and generate a heat‑map of neural activity.

steps.title: Run MATLAB acquisition GUI
steps.instruction: Launch the supplied turn‑key MATLAB graphical user interface, load the Arduino‑shield configuration, and start synchronized acquisition of calcium imaging, pupil video, and locomotion data.

description: This protocol outlines the materials and methods needed to build a head-fixation locomotion wheel adapted for the integration of in vivo multi-photon imaging systems (Figures 1A–1D).1 Our technology is designed to simultaneously monitor pupil dynamics and body movements with an incremental (quadrature) rotary encoder and a pair of CMOS cameras. The frame of our system is built on an optical breadboard, allowing for adjustments of the wheel and headplates during head-fixation. An Arduino microcontroller, connected to a custom printed circuit board (Arduino shield), establishes a digital interface between all the devices in the system and the data acquisition computer. The Arduino shield includes a real-time clock module to provide precise time stamps for all the recorded data and to enable proper synchronization between recorded behavioral and neural data outputs. Additional external triggers on the Arduino shield are available to integrate other widely utilized behavioral or neural acquisition applications. The head-fixation system described in this protocol is a technological solution for parallel measurements of neural, behavior, and physiological data in awake behaving mice. In addition, we provide a turn-key MATLAB graphical user interface (GUI) along with editable scripts to enhance data collection and analysis efficiency, while offering the flexibility to adapt this interface to meet various research needs.Figure 1Head-fixation system with multi-photon imaging configuration(A) Prior to imaging, the objective of the multi-photon system can be raised (∼28 cm difference between air table and bottom of the objective) to provide more space to secure the head-ring between the headplates and ensure a comfortable animal posture.(B) During imaging, the distance between the objective and the head-ring can be adjusted to the imaging depths and the location of the focal plane beneath the implanted surface of the GRIN lens.
